body: CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.
CVE-2026-111357 Ivanti Connect Secure Missing Authentication for Critical Function Vulnerability
CVE-2026-118527 Ivanti Connect Secure Generation of Predictable Numbers or Identifiers Vulnerability
These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Recommended security practices and firewall configurations can help protect an industrial control system network from attacks that originate from outside the network. Such practices include that process control systems are physically protected from direct access by unauthorized personnel, have no direct connections to the Internet, and are separated from other networks by means of a firewall system that has a minimal number of ports exposed, and others that have to be evaluated case by case. Industrial control systems should not be used for Internet surfing, instant messaging, or receiving e-mails. Portable computers and removable storage media should be carefully scanned for viruses before they are connected to a control system. Additional information on Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity Best Practices can be found in the Hitachi Energy’s “Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity Best Practices” Cybersecurity Notification. [1]
CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.
Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet.
Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.

When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.
CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies.
CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets.

Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies.
Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.

title: From industry concern to practical action: the value of working with regulators
summary: How industry, the NCSC and the FCA worked together to help organisations share information while protecting market integrity
body: How industry, the NCSC and the FCA worked together to help organisations share information while protecting market integrity
Sharing cyber incident information quickly, whilst responding to an incident, is an important contributor to UK cyber resilience.

High-profile incidents in the retail sector highlighted the value of timely cyber incident information sharing, not just within the retail sector but with other sectors too. Organisations often rely on the same technologies, suppliers and digital supply chains, meaning an incident affecting one organisation or sector may expose similar vulnerabilities elsewhere. Sharing information enables organisations to learn, adapt and defend themselves against common threats before they cause further harm.

Organisations can share cyber incident information with the NCSC and through trusted information-sharing communities. However, information sharing often takes place under significant operational, legal and commercial pressures. For some organisations, questions about regulatory obligations can create hesitation at exactly the point where timely information may be most valuable to others.

This blog describes how industry, the NCSC and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) worked together to better understand one such challenge, and how that collaboration helped provide greater clarity for organisations seeking to share cyber incident information responsibly.

Organisations recognise the value of sharing information about cyber threats, incidents and mitigations. They understand that doing so can help other organisations protect themselves and strengthen resilience across an entire sector. However, for publicly listed organisations, cyber incidents can also raise questions about market-sensitive or ‘inside’ information and the obligations that come with it.

Some organisations were uncertain about when information could be shared with the NCSC or through trusted information-sharing communities while continuing to meet their obligations under the UK Market Abuse Regulation (MAR), which is overseen by the FCA.
The issue wasn't a lack of willingness to share information; it was uncertainty about how to do so while meeting legal and regulatory obligations.
Rather than treating this solely as a cyber security issue, we brought together the people best placed to understand it from different perspectives.

Industry brought the operational reality of responding to cyber incidents and the practical challenges organisations face when deciding what information can be shared. The NCSC contributed expertise in incident response, trusted information sharing and how the information we receive is used. The FCA – the regulatory body responsible for market-abuse requirements – provided both regulatory expertise and insight into how existing obligations apply in practice during cyber incidents.
Together, we focused on a shared objective: helping organisations understand how they can share cyber incident information while continuing to meet their legal and regulatory obligations.

The discussions showed how collaboration between industry, regulators and cyber security experts can help turn uncertainty into practical guidance. They also demonstrated the role regulators can play in making complex requirements easier to understand and apply.
This work ultimately led to a practical outcome designed to provide greater clarity for organisations seeking to share cyber incident information while meeting their regulatory obligations.
The FCA’s guidance on disclosing inside information relating to cyber incidents helps organisations assess their disclosure obligations when responding to a cyber incident.
Importantly for cyber resilience, it also addresses when organisations may share information with government departments, law enforcement, regulators and trusted information-sharing communities.

The guidance explains that sharing cyber incident information with the NCSC – as part of the NCSC’s work to help protect UK critical systems and online services, and support incident response – may be compatible with an organisation's regulatory obligations. This is because such sharing may be consistent with an organisation acting in the normal exercise of its employment, profession or duties.
It also recognises NCSC-led information-sharing communities where sharing information can help others prevent or mitigate cyber threats.

Individual organisations remain responsible for assessing their own circumstances and meeting their legal and regulatory obligations. However, providing clearer regulatory guidance aims to remove uncertainty that might otherwise discourage appropriate information sharing.
The publication should not be the end of the conversation.
The NCSC and FCA will continue engaging directly with industry, legal advisers and other stakeholders to explain the guidance and understand how it works in practice.

This feedback is important. Cyber incidents don't respect organisational or regulatory boundaries, and building national resilience depends on organisations being able to share information quickly and confidently.

This work is one example of what can be achieved when industry, regulators and cyber security experts come together to address a shared challenge. Sharing cyber incident information with the NCSC and through trusted information-sharing communities remains an important contributor to UK cyber resilience, and we encourage organisations to continue raising any barriers to sharing so they can be better understood, addressed and where possible removed.
Senior Resilience Lead and Cyber Consultant, NCSC

The following versions of Siemens SENTRON 3NA COM Fuse are affected:
Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Transportation Systems, Energy, Healthcare and Public Health, Financial Services, Government Services and Facilities
Vendor fix Update to V5.2 or later version
Relevant CWE: CWE-940 Improper Verification of Source of a Communication Channel
Siemens ProductCERT reported this vulnerability to CISA.

As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurity
For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories
The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use.
CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.
Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet.
Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.

When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.
CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies.
CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets.

Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies.
Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.

title: Critical security issue affecting PHP
summary: Updated: The NCSC is encouraging UK organisations to take immediate action to mitigate a security issue affecting PHP (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619).
body: The NCSC is encouraging UK organisations to take immediate action to mitigate a security issue affecting PHP (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619).
PHP has published a security update to address a critical security issue that may allow attackers to execute commands on any web server running PHP.

PHP (PHP Hypertext Preprocessor) is a widely used server-side scripting language designed for web development. It runs on a web server to generate dynamic page content, interact with databases, and handle backend application logic before delivering the final HTML output to a user's browser. PHP is also used in a range of other products.

The security issue could allow an attacker to trigger an out-of-memory (OOM) condition in PHP that results in memory corruption. Under certain conditions, this corruption could be exploited to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution. This security issue has now been fixed.
CVE-2026-109618: Out-of-memory handling can interrupt PHP while internal request data is only partially initialized. Request cleanup may then treat the invalid data as valid.

CVE-2026-109619: Request-owned internal state can survive after its backing memory has been freed. A later request handled by the same worker may use that stale state before normal initialization resets it.
The full PHP security advisory provides more details regarding the fixed security issue.
The NCSC will continue to monitor for any impact on UK organisations.

Organisations using any version of PHP are affected and all organisations are highly encouraged to update to the latest fixed version. Organisations using older versions of PHP are highly encouraged to update to a fully supported version.
The NCSC recommends following vendor best practice advice in the mitigation of vulnerabilities. The NCSC highly encourages organisations to follow these priority actions:

Identify systems running PHP across your infrastructure, prioritising internet-facing systems. As all versions may be affected, do not limit discovery to outdated PHP versions; identify PHP installations generally and assess their exposure to CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.
Update to the latest version of PHP and continue to monitor for future updates. Prioritise internet-facing systems first and then internal systems.
If you are unable to update to a version with the security update applied, the PHP Foundation have provided temporary mitigations.
If you are unable to apply the temporary mitigations, or applying them would take too long, you should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated.

If you are unable to update or disable the system immediately then you should assess the system for any evidence of compromise prior to your upgrade or mitigation and look for backdoors installed by an attacker. If you are not confident in your ability to do this yourselves then you can get assistance from an NCSC-assured Cyber Incident Response provider.

Continuously monitor for security updates from third-party software vendors, including for appliances and services that may bundle PHP. NCSC-NL have published an inventory list of software products with a PHP dependency potentially affected by the vulnerabilities. Apply relevant updates as they become available.

title: Introducing a new AI chapter in the NCSC research problem book
summary: A revolution is underway at the intersection of AI and cyber security.
body: A revolution is underway at the intersection of AI and cyber security.

The latest frontier AI capabilities are re-writing what is possible for both cyber attackers and defenders, with recent publications from the NCSC highlighting the opportunities and risks presented by AI.

The Five Eyes cyber security agencies have warned that AI is accelerating the pace and scale of cyber threats, while the NCSC’s Cyber Shield initiative sets out an ambitious vision for harnessing AI to strengthen cyber defence.
Turning this vision into reality will require more than advances in AI capability alone; it will require answers to difficult questions around system design, assurance, security and trust.
To help focus innovation across this new AI-enabled world, we’ve re-written our NCSC research problem book to include an entirely new chapter 'AI in cyber security problems’.

For years, AI and machine learning have helped defenders analyse data, identify threats and automate routine tasks. The new generation of AI systems (particularly generative AI and agentic AI) can plan, reason, use tools, and take actions with increasing autonomy. This is game-changing, making some things much easier to automate but in the process, creating new problems to overcome.

Many of the assumptions that underpin today’s cyber security best practice were developed before this kind of AI existed. Concepts such as vulnerability management, incident response and risk management will need to evolve to account for both AI-enabled systems and AI-enabled attackers. This evolution may require a re-design of processes from the ground up to fully leverage the potential benefits to defenders.
Our new problem book chapter on ‘AI in cyber security’ identifies seven areas spanning three broad themes:
the use of AI to strengthen cyber defence
the security and assurance of AI systems themselves
the use of data-driven methods to improve cyber resilience at scale

A common thread runs throughout them all: human-AI collaboration. As AI systems become more capable, we need to understand where autonomy can provide genuine value, where human judgement remains essential, and how meaningful oversight can be maintained without losing the benefits of machine-speed operations.

AI has the potential to fundamentally reshape cyber security. Whether that future is secure, resilient and trustworthy will depend on the choices we make today and the research we undertake tomorrow. The new problem book should focus attention on some of the most important challenges ahead.

Addressing these challenges will require a collective effort across the cyber security and AI communities. We welcome feedback on the challenges identified in the problem book, suggestions for additional research questions, and examples of ongoing or planned research that could help address them. Insights from across academia, industry and government will help ensure that future cyber security approaches remain effective, resilient and trustworthy in an AI-enabled world.
If you would like to contribute to the discussion, please complete our feedback form.
Technical Director for Cyber AI Research, NCSC

title: Post-quantum updates to our TLS guidance
summary: The NCSC publishes its recommendations for configuring post-quantum cryptography in TLS. Now is time to migrate.
body: The NCSC publishes its recommendations for configuring post-quantum cryptography in TLS. Now is time to migrate.

Today we have published our updated guidance on using TLS to protect data, to include recommended configurations for post-quantum cryptography (PQC). This follows the recent publication of RFC 10024 (Post-quantum traditional hybrid key agreement mechanisms for TLS 1.3) by the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force). These configurations are suitable for general use, and for protecting government OFFICIAL information.

We recommend both hybrid post-quantum/traditional and pure post-quantum cipher choices. The hybrid choices are the most widely deployed in commonly-used libraries, but we also recommend configurations that support a pure PQC future.

Some procedural delays have meant that we are still awaiting publication of the final RFC (equivalent to a standard) for pure PQC options. However, stable pure PQC options exist in a number of major libraries, and are available for use.

TLS 1.3 is the only version that supports PQC; earlier versions will not be upgraded. So, if you currently use TLS 1.2 or older versions, you should be moving to TLS 1.3 as soon as possible. As well as supporting quantum resilience, this will give you the much wider set of security benefits that TLS 1.3 offers.

The guidance supports migration to PQC in line with the NCSC's published timelines, in which we recommend that high priority migration activities should be carried out by 2031. For many organisations, protecting the confidentiality of their data in transit will fall into this 'high priority' category, and the availability of standardised post-quantum TLS configurations together with implementations in well-studied libraries, means that you should be aiming to make this move now.

We will continue to provide updates to our technical guidance as PQC support is introduced into particular protocols and product types. In the coming months we plan to update our IPsec guidance as those RFCs are finalised, and to include post-quantum authentication recommendations for TLS.
Principal Technical Director for Crypt and High Threat Technologies, NCSC

title: Using TLS to protect data
summary: Recommended profiles to securely configure TLS for the most common versions and scenarios, with additional guidance for managing older versions.
body: Recommendations for configuring TLS, managing certificates, supporting PQC and deploying secure services.
Avoiding security weaknesses in older versions

This guidance is aimed at system administrators who are responsible for configuring servers or clients within their estate. It explains how to configure TLS securely and transition to post-quantum cryptography (PQC).
transitioning TLS to use PQC, including recommended profiles for its use
configuring TLS 1.3 and TLS 1.2 using recommended cryptographic profiles
managing deprecated protocol versions and disabling known insecure TLS features
deploying TLS for web and mail services
Use the recommended profiles when configuring TLS.
Only TLS 1.3 provides protection against quantum attacks when configured correctly. You can use our recommended TLS 1.3 profiles now.
If you use TLS 1.2, develop a plan to migrate to TLS 1.3 so you can adopt PQC.
Disable TLS 1.1 and TLS 1.0. You must disable all versions of SSL.
You must disable TLS features known to be insecure.
Keep servers and client software up to date. Implementation flaws can introduce vulnerabilities that may be exploited if security updates are not applied promptly.

Transport Layer Security (TLS) is a protocol that provides security for digital communications between two parties. When a server and client communicate, well-configured TLS ensures that no third party can eavesdrop or tamper with any message.
TLS 1.3 is the latest version of TLS. It was designed to be more secure than earlier versions and is the only version that will receive new features in future, such as support for PQC.

TLS 1.2 is still considered to provide strong protection against classical attacks when configured with the recommended cryptographic profiles. However, it will not receive new features apart from critical security updates, as outlined in RFC 9851.
If you use TLS 1.2, you should plan to transition to TLS 1.3 as part of your migration to PQC.
The Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) protocol was the predecessor to TLS. All versions of SSL are deprecated and considered insecure. You must not use them.
TLS 1.1 and 1.0 have also been deprecated by the IETF, as outlined in RFC 8996, and should not be used.
The NCSC recommends that government systems do not support deprecated versions of the protocol, and are upgraded to support TLS 1.3 instead.

A cryptographically-relevant quantum computer would threaten the key exchange and digital signature algorithms currently used to secure TLS. The primary mitigation to this risk is to migrate to PQC, in line with the broader NCSC advice on PQC migration.
RFC 10024 standardises three post-quantum/traditional hybrid key agreement mechanisms in TLS 1.3.
All three are suitable for protecting personal, enterprise and OFFICIAL-tier government information.
These mechanisms combine the post-quantum ML-KEM algorithm with a traditional elliptic curve algorithm. The NCSC recommends using hybrid schemes as an interim measure when migrating to PQC.

The IETF is developing standards for non-hybrid ML-KEM (ML-KEM Post-Quantum Key Agreement for TLS 1.3), which will standardise MLKEM768 and MLKEM1024 as options for TLS. The NCSC considers these algorithms acceptable for use in TLS, and they are already available in many common TLS implementations.

At present, the IETF has only standardised post-quantum algorithms for key exchange in TLS. Work is ongoing to standardise post-quantum authentication in TLS and the wider Web PKI, with a number of drafts at different levels of maturity. Organisations operating private PKIs may be able to adopt post-quantum authentication sooner than services relying on the public Web PKI, where standardisation and wider ecosystem adoption are still ongoing.
Once these standards have been finalised, and mature implementations are available in commercial implementations, this guidance will be updated to include recommendations for their use.
Using cryptographically agile deployments, where it is easier to support alternative cryptographic algorithms, will make these and future transitions easier.

TLS 1.3 introduced some major changes. It uses different cipher suite definitions to earlier TLS versions, and has different configuration options. Some implementations separate TLS 1.3 configuration from previous TLS versions. Please consult your implementation documentation to determine how to configure options specific to TLS 1.3.
The recommended profiles include both post-quantum and traditional algorithms to support the transition to PQC. The recommended symmetric cipher suites are unchanged.

The key exchange algorithms included in the recommended profiles are not the only ones the NCSC considers acceptable. All of the post-quantum key exchange algorithms currently specified for use with TLS 1.3 by the IETF offer appropriate protection for personal, enterprise and OFFICIAL-tier government information.
